output_text: Corbel's zero-shot nDCG@10 gains over Dovetail-DR, the same bi-encoder trained with standard in-batch negatives, averaged 4.7 points across the four held-out collections (40.7 vs 36.0), which is numerically similar to, but not directly comparable with, the 5.2-point improvement reported on a different six-collection suite. Corbel's scores were higher than Dovetail-DR's on every individual collection, with gains ranging from 2.9 points on Brackwater-News (43.1 vs 38.4) to 5.9 points on Moorstone-Bio (50.6 vs 44.7), and higher than Lexi-Sparse's on three of four collections, with the exception of Brackwater-News. Because no statistical tests were reported, the observed differences cannot be characterized as statistically significant, and these findings are limited to the four evaluated collections and a single training run per system.

On the Brightcart-Grocery test set, Bramblewood achieved a mean NDCG@10 of 41.2% (SD 0.7) across 10 seeds, compared to 40.7% (SD 0.6) for Larkspur-Seq. The observed mean difference was 0.5 percentage points; because seeds are paired, a paired test could assess reliability, but none was reported, so this cannot be interpreted as a reliable improvement. Bramblewood's mean NDCG@10 was 22.9 points higher than Most-Popular's 18.3%. These results are specific to Brightcart-Grocery and the leave-last-item-out protocol.

Mosswood achieved the highest test accuracy on Sorrel-Cite (0.837) and Sorrel-Cite-XL (0.791), outperforming Harrier-GCN by 0.023 and 0.029 respectively. On Tamarind-Social, Mosswood's accuracy (0.679) was slightly lower than Harrier-GCN's (0.683), a difference of 0.004. No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be assessed for significance.

Gannet achieved higher success rates than Ledger-RNN on unseen layouts from all three training map families (Warehouse: 88.4% vs 81.2%; Office: 85.1% vs 79.6%; Cavern: 79.3% vs 72.5%). This advantage also held on all three held-out map families (Orchard: 71.6% vs 60.3%; Harbor: 68.2% vs 59.4%; Quarry: 64.9% vs 55.1%), though no statistical tests were reported for these comparisons. Gannet also produced shorter mean episode lengths on successful episodes than Ledger-RNN across all six conditions, with differences ranging from 12 to 21 steps. However, no statistical tests were reported, so these differences are descriptive only.

On the Kestrel-Grid test split, Eddyline achieved a lower MAE than Brenna-ODE (0.212 vs 0.219) while using fewer function evaluations per window (17.8 vs 64). However, Eddyline incurred higher latency than Brenna-ODE on the Halden H5 accelerator (268 ms vs 241 ms per batch of 256 windows). Eddyline also reported a lower MAE than the non-ODE reference Sluice-TCN (0.212 vs 0.231) but at higher latency (268 ms vs 38 ms per batch of 256 windows) on the Halden H5 accelerator.

On Quillbench, Ridgeline-FT achieved a significantly higher pass@1 than Plainweave-FT, with a mean paired difference of 2.26 percentage points (95% CI [1.26, 3.26], Holm-adjusted p = 0.0022). Ridgeline-FT also showed a significantly higher compile rate than Plainweave-FT, with a mean paired difference of 2.7 percentage points (95% CI [1.19, 4.35], Holm-adjusted p = 0.0043). Both fine-tuned recipes outperformed the base model Fernleaf-1.3B on pass@1 (Ridgeline-FT: 47.9% vs 31.4%; Plainweave-FT: 45.6% vs 31.4%) and compile rate (93.1% and 90.4% vs 84.0%), though these comparisons were descriptive only, as no statistical tests were reported.

On the Kestrel-Grid test split, Eddyline achieved a lower MAE than Brenna-ODE (0.212 vs. 0.219) while requiring only 17.8 function evaluations per window compared to Brenna-ODE's fixed 64, and it also reduced median batch latency from 241 ms to 112 ms. Eddyline's latency advantage over Brenna-ODE (112 ms vs. 241 ms) indicates that its higher per-step cost is more than offset by the reduced number of steps, although no statistical tests were reported for these differences. For reference, the non-ODE Sluice-TCN was faster (38 ms) but less accurate (MAE 0.231) than both ODE-based models, and no statistical significance was established for any of the observed differences.

Corbel's zero-shot nDCG@10 gains over Dovetail-DR, the same bi-encoder trained with standard in-batch negatives, averaged 4.7 points across the four held-out collections (40.7 vs 36.0), which is comparable to the 5.2-point average improvement previously reported for denoised hard-negative mining over standard in-batch negatives on a six-collection suite. Corbel outperformed Dovetail-DR on every individual collection, with gains ranging from 2.9 points on Brackwater-News (43.1 vs 38.4) to 5.9 points on Moorstone-Bio (50.6 vs 44.7), and also exceeded the lexical reference Lexi-Sparse on all collections except Brackwater-News. Because no statistical tests were reported, the observed differences cannot be characterized as statistically significant, and the single training run per system limits the strength of any general conclusion.

On the Garnet-Retail test split, Thimble achieves a long-tail Recall@20 of 0.091, compared with 0.085 for Cobble-GNN with debiased sampling and 0.072 for Cobble-GNN with uniform sampling. Adding popularity-debiased negative sampling to Cobble-GNN improves long-tail Recall@20 from 0.072 to 0.085, a relative gain of about 18% on this test split. Thimble's overall Recall@20 (0.219) is slightly higher than Cobble-GNN's (0.214) and Cobble-GNN with debiased sampling (0.212), but no statistical tests were reported, so these differences may not be significant.

Under the stated per-severity interpretation of the pre-specified robustness criterion (drop ≤ 3.0 points), Stellate-Net meets the criterion at blur severities 1 and 3, with mean drops of 0.7 and 1.6 points from its clean accuracy of 94.2%, but fails it at severity 5, where the mean drop is 4.6 points. On the Ostmark-Aerial test split, the reported mean drops for Stellate-Net are smaller than those for Lattice-CNN at all three blur severities (0.7 vs 1.8, 1.6 vs 5.7, and 4.6 vs 11.3 points, respectively). No statistical tests were reported, so these differences in means cannot be claimed as statistically significant.

On the 200 held-out Mirefield levels, Skua achieved a mean success rate of 44.63% ± 3.85% compared with 40.50% ± 4.78% for Plover-PG, a statistically significant improvement (paired t-test, t(9)=4.05, p=0.0029, 95% CI [1.82, 6.44] percentage points). The mean normalized return for Skua (62.95 ± 5.04) was numerically higher than that for Plover-PG (62.04 ± 4.29), but this difference was not statistically significant (paired t-test, t(9)=1.18, p=0.27, 95% CI [-0.84, 2.66]). These results indicate that Skua significantly outperformed Plover-PG on the primary held-out success rate, while the secondary normalized return difference was not statistically significant, with the confidence interval spanning [-0.84, 2.66]. The findings are specific to the 200 held-out Mirefield levels, 25M training steps, and 10 seeds used in this evaluation; the Tally bonus baseline (Plover-PG + Tally bonus) achieved a success rate of 42.10% ± 4.40% and a normalized return of 62.71 ± 3.62, but was not part of the primary comparison.

Glimmer outperforms Trellis-RE on all three test sets, with F1 gains of 3.4 points on Hollin-DocRE (65.2 vs. 61.8), 3.6 points on Saltmarsh-Bio (55.9 vs. 52.3), and 1.1 points on Wistmoor-News (71.1 vs. 70.0). These results are based on mean F1 over three seeds with standard deviations at most 0.4, and no statistical significance tests were reported, so the observed differences should be interpreted with caution.

On the original Tallis-Read test set, Marrowfield-ASR achieved a mean word error rate (WER) of 5.8%, compared to 6.4% for Ostrander-CTC and 6.1% for Pellucid-RNNT. However, the research question concerns robustness to additive background noise, and the supplied evidence contains no evaluations under noisy conditions. Consequently, no claim about Marrowfield-ASR's robustness to additive background noise can be made from the available data.

These results support that Halyard outperforms Tidewell across the evaluated suite, but the claim is limited to these five datasets under the specific setting of horizon 96, z-normalized test MAE, and a 3-seed mean, and no statistical significance tests were reported.

Both models also outperformed the Lead-3 extractive baseline on the held-out scientific domain (36.4% and 34.9% vs 31.7%). However, no statistical tests were reported, so these differences in means are not established as statistically significant.

Marten-GNN achieved higher mean test accuracy than Pinecrest-Conv on all four node-classification graphs, with margins of 1.6, 0.8, 1.5, and 1.1 percentage points on Elmstead-Cite, Harlow-Coauthor, Brack-Social, and Tiller-Protein, respectively. The margins vary across graphs (0.8–1.6 points), and no statistical tests were reported, so the reliability of these improvements cannot be assessed. Marten-GNN also outperformed the feature-only MLP on every graph, with larger margins (10.5, 3.7, 10.6, and 8.6 percentage points), but this does not isolate the effect of graph structure. These results are limited to the evaluated graphs and tuning budgets.

On Halvern-Faces at 256×256 resolution, Sablewing reduces sampling cost by 6.25× in NFE (8 vs. 50) and 5.7× in TFLOPs per image (0.94 vs. 5.40) relative to the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1). Compared with the 10-step truncated Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing is slightly cheaper in TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08) and substantially better in FID (7.8 vs. 15.6), despite using fewer denoising steps (8 vs. 10). No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in FID and cost are descriptive only and cannot be claimed as significant.

On Quillbench, Ridgeline-FT achieved a mean pass@1 of 46.1% ± 1.8% compared with 45.6% ± 1.7% for Plainweave-FT, a difference that was not statistically significant (paired t-test, Holm-adjusted p = 0.36). Ridgeline-FT had a significantly higher mean compile rate than Plainweave-FT (93.1% ± 1.3% vs. 90.4% ± 1.8%; mean paired difference (Ridgeline−Plainweave) 2.77 percentage points, 95% CI [1.19, 4.35], Holm-adjusted p = 0.0087, secondary endpoint). Both fine-tuned variants substantially outperformed the base model Fernleaf-1.3B (31.4% pass@1, 84.0% compile).

Stellate-Net meets the pre-specified robustness criterion (drop ≤ 3.0 points) at blur severities 1 and 3, with top-1 accuracy drops of 0.7 and 1.6 points from clean accuracy, but fails it at severity 5 with a drop of 4.6 points. At every blur severity, Stellate-Net's accuracy drop is smaller than Lattice-CNN's (0.7 vs 1.8 points at severity 1, 1.6 vs 5.7 at severity 3, and 4.6 vs 11.3 at severity 5). Thus, Stellate-Net's robustness to Gaussian blur is partial: it degrades gracefully at low-to-moderate blur but exceeds the 3.0-point threshold at the highest tested severity.

On the Ombria-News test set, Marrowline-int8 achieved a chrF of 57.9 versus 58.4 for Selk-MT, a difference of 0.5 points. In serving latency on the replayed production trace, Marrowline-int8 reduced p50 latency from 186 ms to 97 ms and p99 latency from 1,240 ms to 610 ms compared with Selk-MT. These results indicate that Marrowline-int8 offers substantially lower latency with only a small quality loss relative to the uncompressed production model, although no statistical tests were reported to assess the reliability of these differences.

On the Garnet-Retail test split, Thimble's long-tail Recall@20 of 0.091 exceeds both Cobble-GNN's 0.072 and Cobble-GNN + debiased sampling's 0.085, corresponding to relative gains of 26.4% and 7.1%, respectively. The 18.1% relative improvement in long-tail Recall@20 from Cobble-GNN + debiased sampling (0.085 vs 0.072) is consistent with the roughly 20% relative gains reported by Sorensen-Nakata et al. (2022) for popularity-debiased negative sampling, though that prior work used different datasets. Thimble's overall Recall@20 (0.219) is only slightly higher than Cobble-GNN's (0.214) and Cobble-GNN + debiased sampling's (0.212), with relative differences of at most 2.3%. No statistical tests were reported, so these differences, while directionally consistent with the expected benefits of debiased sampling, should be interpreted cautiously on this single dataset.

Marrowfield-ASR meets the pre-specified robustness criterion of a WER increase of at most 1.5 absolute points at all tested noise levels, with increases of 0.3, 0.9, and 1.3 points at 20, 10, and 5 dB SNR, respectively. Marrowfield-ASR also shows smaller WER increases under noise than Ostrander-CTC at every tested SNR (0.3 vs 1.1 points at 20 dB, 0.9 vs 3.2 at 10 dB, and 1.3 vs 6.6 at 5 dB). On the original clean recordings, Marrowfield-ASR achieves a lower WER (5.8%) than both Ostrander-CTC (6.4%) and Pellucid-RNNT (6.1%), though no statistical tests are reported for any of these comparisons.

Halyard also outperformed the seasonal-naive reference on all five datasets, with margins between 0.055 (Doveton-Weather) and 0.111 (Marrick-Traffic). These results are based on 3-seed means without reported variance, and no statistical significance tests were reported, so the reliability of these differences is not established. The practical importance of the observed MAE gaps is not assessed here and is left to the reader's judgment.

Calloway-Sum outperformed Pellam-Sum on ROUGE-L F1 in all four held-out text domains, with advantages of 1.5 percentage points on Lindqvist-Sci (36.4 vs. 34.9), 1.3 on Corbin-Legal (33.1 vs. 31.8), 1.5 on Ashdown-Meet (29.7 vs. 28.2), and 1.2 on Gable-Reviews (31.5 vs. 30.3). These held-out advantages (1.2–1.5 percentage points) were similar in magnitude to the in-domain advantage of 1.2 percentage points on Ravenmoor News (41.8 vs. 40.6). Calloway-Sum also exceeded the Lead-3 extractive baseline in every held-out domain, with margins of 4.6 percentage points on Gable-Reviews (31.5 vs. 26.9), 4.7 on Lindqvist-Sci (36.4 vs. 31.7), 2.6 on Corbin-Legal (33.1 vs. 30.5), and 7.3 on Ashdown-Meet (29.7 vs. 22.4). Marrowfield-ASR meets the pre-specified robustness criterion at all tested noise levels, with WER increases of 0.3, 0.9, and 1.3 absolute points at 20, 10, and 5 dB SNR, respectively, all within the 1.5-point threshold. In contrast, Ostrander-CTC exceeds the 1.5-point threshold at 10 dB (3.2 points) and 5 dB (6.6 points), indicating that Marrowfield-ASR is more robust to additive background noise than this baseline. However, these findings are limited to the specific noise types, SNRs, and test set evaluated, and no statistical tests were reported to assess the reliability of the observed differences.

Gannet achieved higher success rates than Ledger-RNN on unseen layouts from all three training map families, with margins of 7.2, 5.5, and 6.8 percentage points on Warehouse, Office, and Cavern, respectively. This advantage also held on the three held-out map families evaluated here, where Gannet's success rates were 71.6%, 68.2%, and 64.9% versus Ledger-RNN's 60.3%, 59.4%, and 55.1% on Orchard, Harbor, and Quarry, respectively. Among successful episodes, Gannet also produced shorter mean episode lengths across all six evaluation conditions, with reductions ranging from 11 to 21 steps, averaged over 5 seeds. Marten-GNN outperformed Pinecrest-Conv on Elmstead-Cite (84.7 ± 0.5% vs 83.1 ± 0.6%) and Harlow-Coauthor (92.6 ± 0.3% vs 91.8 ± 0.4%), but Pinecrest-Conv achieved higher accuracy on Brack-Social (70.4 ± 0.9% vs 69.8 ± 0.9%) and Tiller-Protein (76.2 ± 0.7% vs 75.5 ± 0.7%). Thus, Marten-GNN did not consistently outperform Pinecrest-Conv across the four graphs, winning on two and losing on two. Glimmer (full) achieves higher relation F1 than Trellis-RE on Hollin-DocRE (65.2% vs 61.8%) and Saltmarsh-Bio (55.9% vs 52.3%), but lower F1 on Wistmoor-News (69.2% vs 70.0%). Removing the evidence-gating module decreases F1 on Hollin-DocRE (63.0% vs 65.2%) and Saltmarsh-Bio (54.1% vs 55.9%), but increases F1 on Wistmoor-News (72.4% vs 69.2%). Thus, the evidence-gating module's benefit is inconsistent across domains: it improves performance in the in-domain and biomedical settings but hurts performance on the news test set. On the Ombria-News test set, Marrowline-int8 achieved a chrF of 57.9 versus 58.4 for Selk-MT, a decrease of 0.5 points. In serving latency on the replayed production trace, Marrowline-int8 reduced p50 latency from 186 ms to 97 ms and p99 latency from 1,240 ms to 610 ms compared with Selk-MT. On the Brightcart-Grocery test period, Bramblewood achieved a higher NDCG@10 than Larkspur-Seq (41.2% vs 40.7%), a mean paired difference of 0.5 percentage points that was statistically significant (paired t-test, p=0.0043, 95% CI [0.21, 0.85]). Both neural models achieved higher mean NDCG@10 than the non-personalized Most-Popular baseline (41.2% and 40.7% vs 18.3%) and higher mean Recall@20 (63.8% and 63.1% vs 37.9%) on the Brightcart-Grocery test period, though no statistical test was reported for these comparisons.

Sablewing is substantially more efficient than Ordell-DDS for 256×256 face generation, reducing NFE from 50 to 8, TFLOPs per image from 5.40 to 0.94, and wall-clock time from 21.7 s to 3.9 s per batch of 64, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1). Compared to Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing uses fewer NFE (8 vs. 10) and slightly lower TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08) and wall-clock time (3.9 s vs. 4.5 s), while achieving a much lower FID (7.8 vs. 15.6). On the original Tallis-Read test set, Marrowfield-ASR achieved a lower word error rate (5.8%) than both Ostrander-CTC (6.4%) and Pellucid-RNNT (6.1%), though no statistical tests were reported for these comparisons. The research question regarding robustness to additive background noise cannot be answered from the supplied evidence, as only original recordings were evaluated and no noise-added conditions or robustness criterion were applied.

Thimble's additional gain over the debiased-sampling baseline (0.091 vs 0.085) suggests that its session-aware encoder provides a further long-tail benefit, but this improvement is modest and not statistically verified.

Because no statistical tests were reported, the observed differences cannot be characterized as statistically significant, and the single training run per system limits the strength of any general conclusion.

Lattice-CNN, by contrast, exceeds the 3.0-point threshold at severities 3 and 5 (drops of 5.7 and 11.3 points) while remaining within it at severity 1 (1.8 points). Stellate-Net's clean accuracy (94.2%) is also higher than Lattice-CNN's (93.6%), providing context for interpreting the drop magnitudes. No statistical tests were reported, so these findings are limited to the tested severities and dataset, and no significance claims are made.

On the held-out Lindqvist-Sci scientific-article domain, Calloway-Sum achieved a higher mean ROUGE-L F1 (36.4%) than Pellam-Sum (34.9%), indicating that its advantage over Pellam-Sum extends to this single scientific-article domain. The observed advantage on Lindqvist-Sci (1.5 percentage points) is larger than the in-domain advantage on Ravenmoor News (1.2 percentage points), but no statistical test was reported, so the reliability of these differences is not established. Both models showed higher mean ROUGE-L F1 than the Lead-3 extractive baseline on the held-out domain (31.7%), but these results are limited to a single scientific-article dataset and to the ROUGE-L metric, and no statistical tests support the observed differences.

On Garnet-Retail, Thimble achieved a long-tail Recall@20 of 0.091, compared to 0.085 for Cobble-GNN with debiased sampling and 0.072 for Cobble-GNN with uniform sampling, corresponding to relative long-tail gains of 26.4% and 18.1% over the uniform baseline, respectively. The 18.1% long-tail gain from debiased sampling alone cannot be directly compared to prior work, as Sorensen-Nakata et al. (2022) report only a 21% reduction in training time and less than 1% change in overall Recall@20, with no long-tail Recall@20 results. Thimble showed a higher mean long-tail Recall@20 than the debiased-sampling baseline, but this difference is unverified due to the absence of statistical tests and the use of a single dataset.

On Halvern-Faces at 256×256 resolution, Sablewing reduces sampling cost by 5.7× in NFE (8 vs. 50) and 5.7× in TFLOPs per image (0.94 vs. 5.40) relative to the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1). Compared with the 10-step truncated Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing is slightly cheaper in TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08) and substantially better in FID (7.8 vs. 15.6), despite using fewer denoising steps (8 vs. 10). No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in FID and cost are descriptive only and cannot be claimed as significant.

Glimmer outperforms Trellis-RE on the in-domain Hollin-DocRE set (65.2% vs. 61.8% F1) and on the biomedical Saltmarsh-Bio set (55.9% vs. 52.3% F1), but underperforms on the news Wistmoor-News set (69.2% vs. 70.0% F1). The ablation shows that removing the evidence-gating module reduces F1 on Hollin-DocRE (from 65.2% to 63.0%) and Saltmarsh-Bio (from 55.9% to 54.1%), but increases F1 on Wistmoor-News (from 69.2% to 72.4%). No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be characterized as significant or reliable.

On the Brightcart-Grocery test set, Bramblewood achieved a mean NDCG@10 of 41.2% (SD 0.7) across 10 seeds, compared to 40.7% (SD 0.6) for Larkspur-Seq. This corresponds to a mean improvement of 0.5 percentage points for Bramblewood over Larkspur-Seq, but no statistical test was reported, so the difference cannot be characterized as significant. Both neural models substantially outperformed the non-personalized Most-Popular baseline, which reached an NDCG@10 of 18.3%.

On the Kestrel-Grid test split, Eddyline achieved a lower MAE than Brenna-ODE (0.212 vs. 0.219) while using fewer function evaluations per forecast window (17.8 vs. 64). However, Eddyline's median latency per batch of 256 windows was higher than Brenna-ODE's (268 ms vs. 241 ms), consistent with Eddyline's higher per-step cost from its controller network and implicit correction solve. Eddyline also had a lower MAE than the non-ODE reference Sluice-TCN (0.212 vs. 0.231) but was markedly slower (268 ms vs. 38 ms per batch). No statistical tests were reported, so these differences are descriptive and not established as significant.

Glimmer achieves higher mean F1 than Trellis-RE on all three test sets, with gains of 3.4 points on Hollin-DocRE (65.2 vs. 61.8), 3.6 points on Saltmarsh-Bio (55.9 vs. 52.3), and 1.1 points on Wistmoor-News (71.1 vs. 70.0). The ablation shows that removing the evidence-gating module reduces F1 on Hollin-DocRE and Saltmarsh-Bio (from 65.2 to 63.0 and from 55.9 to 54.1, respectively), but increases F1 on Wistmoor-News by 1.3 points (from 71.1 to 72.4), indicating that the gating module's benefit is not universal. All systems were trained only on Hollin-DocRE, so the out-of-domain results on Saltmarsh-Bio and Wistmoor-News should be interpreted with that scope in mind. No statistical significance tests were reported, so the observed differences should be interpreted with caution.

On the Brightcart-Grocery test set, Bramblewood achieved a mean NDCG@10 of 41.2% (SD 0.7) across 10 seeds, compared with 40.7% (SD 0.6) for Larkspur-Seq. A paired t-test (n=10, paired by seed) showed that this difference was statistically significant (t=3.79, df=9, p=0.0043, 95% CI [0.21, 0.85] percentage points), indicating that Bramblewood outperformed Larkspur-Seq in NDCG@10 on this dataset. Both neural models achieved higher NDCG@10 than the non-personalized Most-Popular baseline (Bramblewood 41.2%, Larkspur-Seq 40.7%, vs Most-Popular 18.3%) on this dataset.

Corbel's zero-shot nDCG@10 averaged 40.7 across the four held-out collections, exceeding Dovetail-DR's 36.0 by 4.7 points. This gain is comparable to the 5.2-point improvement previously reported for denoised hard-negative mining on a biomedical collection, though the present comparison is on a different collection and no statistical test was reported. Corbel also outperformed the lexical reference Lexi-Sparse by 5.4 points on average (40.7 vs. 35.3), with gains on all four collections.

On Quillbench, Ridgeline-FT achieved a mean pass@1 of 46.1% ± 1.8% compared with 45.6% ± 1.7% for Plainweave-FT, a difference that was not statistically significant (paired t-test, Holm-adjusted p = 0.36). Ridgeline-FT showed a significantly higher compile rate than Plainweave-FT (93.1% ± 1.3% vs. 90.4% ± 1.8%; mean paired difference 2.77 percentage points, 95% CI [1.19, 4.35], Holm-adjusted p = 0.0087). Thus, the evidence supports a benefit of Ridgeline-FT over Plainweave-FT in compile rate but not in pass@1 on this benchmark.

On unseen layouts from the three training map families, Gannet achieved higher success rates than Ledger-RNN (Warehouse: 88.4% vs 81.2%; Office: 85.1% vs 79.6%; Cavern: 79.3% vs 72.5%) and shorter mean episode lengths on successful episodes (Warehouse: 142 vs 158 steps; Office: 151 vs 163 steps; Cavern: 177 vs 189 steps). These results indicate that Gannet's advantage over Ledger-RNN generalizes to unseen layouts within the same map families it was trained on. However, because no statistical tests were reported and the evaluation was limited to the training map families, the evidence does not establish generalization to map families beyond those used in training.

This efficiency gain comes at a modest sample-quality cost, with FID increasing from 7.1 for Ordell-DDS to 7.8 for Sablewing. Compared with the 10-step Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing is both more efficient (8 vs 10 NFE, 0.94 vs 1.08 TFLOPs, 3.9 vs 4.5 s per batch) and better in quality (FID 7.8 vs 15.6). No statistical tests were reported, and these results are limited to a single dataset and setting.

Corbel outperformed Dovetail-DR on all four held-out collections, with per-collection gains ranging from 3.8 points on Felloe-Fin (35.0 vs 31.2) to 5.9 points on Moorstone-Bio (50.6 vs 44.7). Corbel also exceeded the lexical reference Lexi-Sparse on average (40.7 vs 35.3) and on every collection, with the largest margin on Felloe-Fin (35.0 vs 27.9, +7.1 points).

On the Ombria-News test set, Marrowline-int8 achieved a chrF of 57.9 versus 58.4 for Selk-MT, a difference of 0.5 points. These findings are specific to the Ombria-News test set and the Pellmar P2 trace, and without statistical tests the practical significance of these differences cannot be assessed.
